walkthrough:
What an allele really is**
Think of a gene as a fixed position on a chromosome that codes for one feature, such as eye colour. An allele is just one version of that gene. Here the eye-colour gene has two versions, R for red and r for purple, occupying the same locus on homologous chromosomes.

What dominant means**
Dominant describes an allele whose effect masks the other allele when both are present. So Rr flies have red eyes, not pink or purple, because R is expressed in the heterozygote and determines the phenotype. The recessive r only shows when homozygous as rr.
Final answer: allele: a variant / different form of a gene; dominant: an allele that is always expressed in the phenotype / expressed in the heterozygote.

walkthrough:
Write the parents**
The wild type parent looks normal, so its phenotype is red eyes and long wings. The question tells you it is heterozygous for both genes, so its genotype must be RrNn. The other parent is homozygous recessive for both genes, so its phenotype is the double mutant purple eyes and vestigial wings, genotype rrnn.

Read the offspring phenotypes from the drawings**
Work left to right. Fly 1 has dark eyes and long wings over the abdomen: red eye, long wing. Fly 2 has pale eyes and short wings: purple eye, vestigial wing. Fly 3 has dark eyes and short wings: red eye, vestigial wing. Fly 4 has pale eyes and long wings: purple eye, long wing.

Deduce the offspring genotypes**
This is a test cross. The rrnn parent only makes rn gametes, so the offspring genotype directly reveals the gamete from the RrNn parent. RN + rn gives RrNn (red-long), rn + rn gives rrnn (purple-vestigial), Rn + rn gives Rrnn (red-vestigial), rN + rn gives rrNn (purple-long). The large numbers 1339 and 1195 correspond to the first two parental-type classes.

Final answer: parental phenotype: wild type parent red eye, long wing x double recessive parent purple eye, vestigial wing; parental genotype: RrNn x rrnn; offspring phenotypes left to right: red eye, long wing; purple eye, vestigial wing; red eye, vestigial wing; purple eye, long wing; offspring genotypes left to right: RrNn; rrnn; Rrnn; rrNn.

Compare the numbers 1339 and 1195 with 151 and 154 - which two phenotypes are parental combinations and which two must be new recombinant combinations?
Think about the only way linked alleles can be reshuffled onto new chromatids during meiosis to make those few recombinant offspring.
walkthrough:
Linkage prevents independent assortment**
If the genes were on different chromosomes, the RrNn parent would make four gamete types RN, rn, Rn, rN in equal numbers by independent assortment, giving 1:1:1:1 in this test cross. Here both genes are on the same chromosome, so R is physically linked to N and r is linked to n. They tend to be inherited together.

Use the numbers as evidence**
You see about 2534 parental-type offspring (1339 red-long and 1195 purple-vestigial) but only about 305 recombinant offspring (151 red-vestigial and 154 purple-long). That large excess of parental types and shortage of recombinants is the classic signature of linkage.

Explain the rare recombinants**
The few recombinant gametes Rn and rN are produced when homologous chromosomes exchange segments by crossing over during prophase I of meiosis. That breaks the original RN and rn combinations and creates new chromosome combinations, but it is infrequent, so recombinant phenotypes stay rare.

Final answer: the two genes are linked on the same chromosome / alleles inherited together, so no independent assortment; most offspring are parental types (1339 and 1195) and few are recombinants (151 and 154); recombinants arise by crossing over between homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis / gamete formation.
